title: Islam is built on five
hookLine: Islam is built on five: the testimony, prayer, zakat, Hajj and the fast
carry: built on five pillars, every one needed
tomorrow: before your first breath, what was already written down?
last: HE CAME TO TEACH YOU YOUR RELIGION.

cards: Somebody posts a song's lyrics with two lines swapped, and the comments go to war. Same words, same song. Does the order matter?
Yesterday's question asked what holds the building of Islam up. Abdullah ibn Umar reports the answer from the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: Islam is built on five.
Testifying that there's no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His messenger. Prayer. Zakat.
Hajj. And the fast of Ramadan. Five pillars, and a building on top.

teach.b: A man repeats it back: Hajj, and the fast of Ramadan. Ibn Umar stops him. No: the fast of Ramadan, and Hajj.
That's how I heard it from the Messenger of Allah. So, does the order matter? Here are two views, and each has a real case.
The first is Ibn Umar's own. A report is a trust.

teach.h: VIEW ONE: CARRY IT AS IT CAME.
teach.b: The words came from the Prophet, so you carry them the way they came, order and all, because a small slip today is a different report tomorrow.
The second: what you pass on is the meaning. Five pillars, none missing, and the building stands the same either way.
Hadith scholars discussed reporting by meaning, and some allowed it for a careful narrator who knew the language well. Now the detail to tell a friend tonight.
In Sahih al-Bukhari, the same hadith from Ibn Umar lists Hajj before the fast. Both orders sit in the sahih collections, and commentators have offered more than one way to fit them together.
Under the argument, both sides agree on the picture: a building on five, and every pillar needed for it to stand. The debate is only about how carefully you carry the blueprint.

how: Muslim children learn the five pillars among their first lessons, sometimes counting them on one hand, and some classes memorize this hadith in Arabic.

games.why: his case is about faithfully passing it on: 'that's how I heard it.' the other side's best case is that the meaning, all five pillars, stays whole either way.

practice: Hold up one hand. Fold down a finger for each pillar as you name it: the testimony, prayer, zakat, the fast, Hajj.
Then go back through them slowly, and for each one, let a face come to mind, someone you've seen pray, give, fast or travel for it, until the hand is closed.

wordCard.voice: Built on five: Islam pictured as a building on five pillars, the testimony, prayer, zakat, the fast and Hajj, in whichever order they reached you.

orig.note: Arabic: Islam is built on five, the opening words of the hadith.

carryVoice: Keep this one close: built on five pillars, every one needed, whichever order you heard them in. That's the third hadith, read.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 16 (Islam built on five; the man who said 'Hajj and the fast', and Ibn Umar's correction)
